name: A Heap of Heaps
description: Andrew skipped lessons on the subject 'Algorithms and Data Structures' for the entire term. When he came to the final test, the teacher decided to give him a difficult task as a punishment. The teacher gave Andrew an array of n numbers a 1 , ... , a n . After that he asked Andrew for each k from 1 to n - 1 to build a k -ary heap on the array and count the number of elements for which the property of the minimum-rooted heap is violated, i.e. the value of an element is less than the value of its parent. Andrew looked up on the Wikipedia that a k -ary heap is a rooted tree with vertices in elements of the array. If the elements of the array are indexed from 1 to n , then the children of element v are elements with indices k ( v - 1) + 2 , ... , kv + 1 (if some of these elements lie outside the borders of the array, the corresponding children are absent). In any k -ary heap every element except for the first one has exactly one parent; for the element 1 the parent is absent (this element is the root of the heap). Denote p ( v ) as the number of the parent of the element with the number v . Let's say that for a non-root element v the property of the heap is violated if a v < a p ( v ) . Help Andrew cope with the task!
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer n ( 2 ≤ n ≤ 2·10 5 ). The second line contains n space-separated integers a 1 , ... , a n ( - 10 9 ≤ a i ≤ 10 9 ).
output_specification: in a single line print n - 1 integers, separate the consecutive numbers with a single space — the number of elements for which the property of the k -ary heap is violated, for k = 1 , 2 , ... , n - 1 .
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 538F — A Heap of Heaps [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
